lessons.title: What is Terraform?
lessons.explanation: Terraform is an infrastructure as code (IaC) tool that lets you build, change, and version cloud and on-premise resources safely and efficiently. It uses a declarative configuration language called HCL (HashiCorp Configuration Language).
lessons.why: It allows teams to manage their infrastructure as if it were application code, enabling version control, testing, and continuous integration/deployment.
lessons.mentalModel: HCL Config (Your Intent) → Terraform (The Engine) → State File (The Reality) → Cloud Provider (The Destination)
lessons.productionNote: Always pin your provider versions to prevent breaking changes when you run a new Terraform init.
lessons.takeaway: Terraform translates your desired state configuration into the API calls necessary to create it.

lessons.title: The Core Workflow
lessons.explanation: The core Terraform workflow consists of four main stages: Write, Init, Plan, and Apply. Understanding this cycle is critical.
lessons.why: This process ensures that your infrastructure changes are safe, validated, and predictable.
lessons.mentalModel: WRITE (.tf files) → INIT (download plugins) → PLAN (preview changes) → APPLY (make the changes) → STATE (update mapping)
lessons.exampleCode:
Step 1: Write a simple .tf file
Step 2: Run 'terraform init'
Step 3: Run 'terraform plan' to see what will happen
Step 4: Run 'terraform apply' and confirm with 'yes'
lessons.productionNote: In CI/CD, you should run 'terraform plan -out=tfplan' and then use 'terraform apply tfplan' to guarantee that the changes reviewed are exactly what get applied.
lessons.takeaway: Init, Plan, Apply is the mantra of infrastructure deployment with Terraform.

lessons.title: Input Variables
lessons.explanation: Input variables serve as parameters for your Terraform modules, allowing you to reuse configurations across different environments without hard-coding values.
lessons.why: Variables make your configurations dynamic and reusable. Without them, you'd need separate .tf files for every environment (dev, test, prod).
lessons.productionNote: Use validation blocks in your variables to enforce constraints early on. Example: ensure a VM name starts with 'vm-'.
lessons.takeaway: Variables are parameters that make your modules reusable and dynamic.
